entries.d043b63cb8af055eea4885e217db9da43889c69f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv115"/><title type="x-ms">Galatians</title> <div sID="gen31653" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31654" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">This</hi> epistle of Paul is directed not to the church or churches of a single city, as some others are, but of a country or province, for so Galatia was. It is very probable that these Galatians were first converted to the Christian faith by his ministry; or, if he was not the instrument of planting, yet at least he had been employed in watering these churches, as is evident from this epistle itself, and also from <reference osisRef="Acts.18.23">Acts xviii. 23</reference>, where we find him going over all the country of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples. While he was with them, they had expressed the greatest esteem and affection both for his person and ministry; but he had not been long absent from them before some judaizing teachers got in among them, by whose arts and insinuations they were soon drawn into a meaner opinion both of the one and of the other. That which these false teachers chiefly aimed at was to draw them off from the truth as it is in Jesus, particularly in the great doctrine of justification, which they grossly perverted, by asserting the necessity of joining the observance of the law of Moses with faith in Christ in order to it: and, the better to accomplish this their design, they did all they could to lessen the character and reputation of the apostle, and to raise up their own on the ruins of his, representing him as one who, if he was to be owned as an apostle, yet was much inferior to others, and particularly who deserved not such a regard as Peter, James, and John, whose followers, it is likely, they pretended to be: and in both these attempts they had but too great success. This was the occasion of his writing this epistle, wherein he expresses his great concern that they had suffered themselves to be so soon turned aside from the faith of the gospel, vindicates his own character and authority as an apostle against the aspersions of his enemies, showing that his mission and doctrine were both divine, and that he was not, upon any account, <hi type="italic">behind the very chief of the apostles,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.5">2 Cor. xi. 5</reference>. He then sets himself to assert and maintain the great gospel doctrine of justification by faith without the works of the law, and to obviate some difficulties that might be apt to arise in their minds concerning it: and, having established this important doctrine, he exhorts them to stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ had made them free, cautions them against the abuse of this liberty, gives them several very needful counsels and directions and then concludes the epistle by giving them a just description of those false teachers by whom they had been ensnared, and, on the contrary, of his own temper and behaviour. In all this his great scope and design were to recover those who had been perverted, to settle those who might be wavering, and to confirm such among them as had kept their integrity. <div eID="gen31654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31655" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31656" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, after the preface or introduction (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.1-Gal.1.5">ver. 1-5</reference>), the apostle severely reproves these churches for their defection from the faith (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.6-Gal.1.9">ver. 6-9</reference>), and then proves his own apostleship, which his enemies had brought them to question, I. From his end and design in preaching the gospel, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.10">ver. 10</reference>. II. From his having received it by immediate revelation, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.11-Gal.1.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. For the proof of which he acquaints them, 1. What his former conversation was, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.13-Gal.1.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>. 2. How he was converted, and called to the apostleship, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.15-Gal.1.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>. 3. How he behaved himself afterwards, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.16-Gal.1.24">ver. 16, to the end</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv115"/> <div eID="gen31656" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31655" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Introductory Address. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 56.)</title> <div sID="gen31657" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Paul, an apostle, (not of men, neither by man, but by Jesus Christ, and God the Father, who raised him from the dead;) <hi type="super">2</hi> And all the brethren which are with me, unto the churches of Galatia: <hi type="super">3</hi> Grace <hi type="italic">be</hi> to you and peace from God the Father, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> our Lord Jesus Christ, <hi type="super">4</hi> Who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present evil world, according to the will of God and our Father: 5 To whom <hi type="italic">be</hi> glory for ever and ever. Amen. <div eID="gen31657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31658" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have the preface or introduction to the epistle, where observe, <div eID="gen31658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31659" type="x-p"/> I. The person or persons from whom this epistle is sent—from Paul <hi type="italic">an apostle,</hi> &c., <hi type="italic">and all the brethren that were with him.</hi> 1. The epistle is sent from Paul; he only was the penman of it. And, because there were some among the Galatians who endeavoured to lessen his character and authority, in the front of it he gives a general account both of his office and of the manner in which he was called to it, which afterwards, in this and the following chapter, he enlarges more upon. As to his office, he was an apostle. He is not afraid to style himself so, though his enemies would scarcely allow him this title: and, to let them see that he did not assume this character without just ground, he acquaints them how he was called to this dignity and office, and assures them that his commission to it was wholly divine, for he was an apostle, <hi type="italic">not of man, neither by man;</hi> he had not the common call of an ordinary minister, but an extraordinary call from heaven to this office. He neither received his qualification for it, nor his designation to it, by the mediation of men, but had both the one and the other directly from above; for he was an apostle <hi type="italic">by Jesus Christ,</hi> he had his instructions and commission immediately from him, and consequently from <hi type="italic">God the Father,</hi> who was one with him in respect of his divine nature, and who had appointed him, as Mediator, to be the apostle and high priest of our profession, and as such to authorize others to this office. He adds, <hi type="italic">Who raised him from the dead,</hi> both to acquaint us that herein God the Father gave a public testimony to Christ's being his Son and the promised Messiah, and also that, as his call to the apostleship was immediately from Christ, so it was after his resurrection from the dead, and when he had entered upon his exalted state; so that he had reason to look upon himself, not only as standing upon a level with the other apostles, but as in some sort preferred above them; for, whereas they were called by him when on earth, he had his call from him when in heaven. Thus does the apostle, being constrained to it by his adversaries, magnify his office, which shows that though men should by no means be proud of any authority they are possessed of, yet at certain times and upon certain occasions it may become needful to assert it. But, 2. He joins all the brethren that were with him in the inscription of the epistle, and writes in their name as well as his own. By <hi type="italic">the brethren that were with him</hi> may be understood either the Christians in common of that place where he now was, or such as were employed as ministers of the gospel. These, notwithstanding his own superior character and attainments, he is ready to own as his brethren; and, though he alone wrote the epistle, yet he joins them with himself in the inscription of it. Herein, as he shows his own great modesty and humility, and how remote he was from an assuming temper, so he might do this to dispose these churches to a greater regard to what he wrote, since hereby it would appear that he had their concurrence with him in the doctrine which he had preached, and was now about to confirm, and that it was no other than what was both published and professed by others as well as himself. <div eID="gen31659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31660" type="x-p"/> II. To whom this epistle is sent—<hi type="italic">to the churches of Galatia.</hi> There were several churches at that time in this country, and it should seem that all of them were more or less corrupted through the arts of those seducers who had crept in among them; and therefore Paul, on whom <hi type="italic">came daily the care of all the churches,</hi> being deeply affected with their state, and concerned for their recovery to the faith and establishment in it, writes this epistle to them. He directs it to all of them, as being all more or less concerned in the matter of it; and he gives them the name of <hi type="italic">churches,</hi> though they had done enough to forfeit it, for corrupt churches are never allowed to be churches: no doubt there were some among them who still continued in the faith, and he was not without hope that others might be recovered to it. <div eID="gen31660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31661" type="x-p"/> III. The apostolical benediction, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.3">v. 3</reference>. Herein the apostle, and the brethren who were with him, wish these churches <hi type="italic">grace and peace from God the Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> This is the usual blessing wherewith he blesses the churches in the name of the Lord—<hi type="italic">grace and peace.</hi> Grace includes God's good-will towards us and his good work upon us; and peace implies in it all that inward comfort, or outward prosperity, which is really needful for us; and they come from God the Father as the fountain, through Jesus Christ as the channel of conveyance. Both these the apostle wishes for these Christians. But we may observe, First grace, and then peace, for there can be no true peace without grace. Having mentioned the Lord Jesus Christ, he cannot pass without enlarging upon his love; and therefore adds (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">Who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver,</hi> &c. Jesus Christ gave himself for our sins, as a great sacrifice to make atonement for us; this the justice of God required, and to this he freely submitted for our sakes. One great end hereof was <hi type="italic">to deliver us from this present evil world;</hi> not only to redeem us from the wrath of God, and the curse of the law, but also to recover us from the corruption that is in the world through lust, and to rescue us from the vicious practices and customs of it, unto which we are naturally enslaved; and possibly also to set us free from the Mosaic constitution, for so <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">aion houtos</hi></hi> is used, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">1 Cor. ii. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">8</reference>. From this we may note, 1. This present world is an evil world: it has become so by the sin of man, and it is so on account of the sin and sorrow with which it abounds and the many snares and temptations to which we are exposed as long as we continue in it. But, 2. Jesus Christ has died to deliver us from this present evil world, not presently to remove his people out of it, but to rescue them from the power of it, to keep them from the evil of it, and in due time to possess them of another and better world. This, the apostle informs us, he has done <hi type="italic">according to the will of God and our Father.</hi> In offering up himself a sacrifice for this end and purpose, he acted by the appointment of the Father, as well as with his own free consent; and therefore we have the greatest reason to depend upon the efficacy and acceptableness of what he has done and suffered for us; yea, hence we have encouragement to look upon God as our Father, for thus the apostle here represents him: as he is the Father of our Lord Jesus, so in and through him he is also the Father of all true believers, as our blessed Saviour himself acquaints us (<reference osisRef="John.20.17">John xx. 17</reference>), when he tells his disciples that he was ascending to his Father and their Father. <div eID="gen31661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31662" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having thus taken notice of the great love wherewith Christ hath loved us, concludes this preface with a solemn ascription of praise and glory to him (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">To whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.</hi> Intimating that on this account he is justly entitled to our highest esteem and regard. Or this doxology may be considered as referring both to God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom he had just before been wishing grace and peace. They are both the proper objects of our worship and adoration, and all honour and glory are perpetually due to them, both on account of their own infinite excellences, and also on account of the blessings we receive from them.
entries.aa3042c742954f4aa59a9037b18047962e74837f: <div eID="gen31662" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Concern at Their Defection. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 56.)</title> <div sID="gen31663" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel: 7 Which is not another; but there be some that trouble you, and would pervert the gospel of Christ. <hi type="super">8</hi> But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed. <hi type="super">9</hi> As we said before, so say I now again, If any <hi type="italic">man</hi> preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed. <div eID="gen31663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31664" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle comes to the body of the epistle; and he begins it with a more general reproof of these churches for their unsteadiness in the faith, which he afterwards, in some following parts of it, enlarges more upon. Here we may observe, <div eID="gen31664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31665" type="x-p"/> I. How much he was concerned at their defection: <hi type="italic">I marvel,</hi> &c. It filled him at once with the greatest surprise and sorrow. Their sin and folly were that they did not hold fast the doctrine of Christianity as it had been preached to them, but suffered themselves to be removed from the purity and simplicity of it. And there were several things by which their defection was greatly aggravated; as, 1. That they were <hi type="italic">removed from him that had called them;</hi> not only from the apostle, who had been the instrument of calling them into the fellowship of the gospel, but from God himself, by whose order and direction the gospel was preached to them, and they were invited to a participation of the privileges of it: so that herein they had been guilty of a great abuse of his kindness and mercy towards them. 2. That they had been <hi type="italic">called into the grace of Christ.</hi> As the gospel which had been preached to them was the most glorious discovery of divine grace and mercy in Christ Jesus; so thereby they had been called to partake of the greatest blessings and benefits, such as justification, and reconciliation with God here, and eternal life and happiness hereafter. These our Lord Jesus has purchased for us at the expense of his precious blood, and freely bestows upon all who sincerely accept of him: and therefore, in proportion to the greatness of the privilege they enjoyed, such were their sin and folly in deserting it and suffering themselves to be drawn off from the established way of obtaining these blessings. 3. That they were <hi type="italic">so soon removed.</hi> In a very little time they lost that relish and esteem of this grace of Christ which they seemed to have, and too easily fell in with those who taught justification by the works of the law, as many did, who had been bred up in the opinions and notions of the Pharisees, which they mingled with the doctrine of Christ, and so corrupted it; and this, as it was an instance of their weakness, so it was a further aggravation of their guilt. 4. That they were removed to <hi type="italic">another gospel, which yet was not another.</hi> Thus the apostle represents the doctrine of these judaizing teachers; he calls it another gospel, because it opened a different way of justification and salvation from that which was revealed in the gospel, namely, by works, and not by faith in Christ. And yet he adds, "<hi type="italic">Which is not another</hi>—you will find it to be no gospel at all—not really another gospel, but the perverting of the gospel of Christ, and the overturning of the foundations of that"—whereby he intimates that those who go about to establish any other way to heaven than what the gospel of Christ has revealed are guilty of a gross perversion of it, and in the issue will find themselves wretchedly mistaken. Thus the apostle endeavours to impress upon these Galatians a due sense of their guilt in forsaking the gospel way of justification; and yet at the same time he tempers his reproof with mildness and tenderness towards them, and represents them as rather drawn into it by the arts and industry of some that troubled them than as coming into it of their own accord, which, though it did not excuse them, yet was some extenuation of their fault. And hereby he teaches us that, in reproving others, as we should be faithful, so we should also be gentle, and endeavour <hi type="italic">to restore them in the spirit of meekness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.1">ch. vi. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen31665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31666" type="x-p"/> II. How confident he was that the gospel he had preached to them was the only true gospel. He was so fully persuaded of this that he pronounced an anathema upon those who pretended to preach any other gospel (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.8">v. 8</reference>), and, to let them see that this did not proceed from any rashness or intemperate zeal in him, he repeated it, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.9">v. 9</reference>. This will not justify our thundering out anathemas against those who differ from us in minor things. It is only against those who forge a new gospel, who overturn the foundation of the covenant of grace, by setting up the works of the law in the place of Christ's righteousness, and corrupting Christianity with Judaism, that Paul denounces this. He puts the case: "Suppose we should preach any other gospel; nay, suppose an angel from heaven should:" not as if it were possible for an angel from heaven to be the messenger of a lie; but it is expressed so the more to strengthen what he was about to say. "If you have any other gospel preached to you by any other person, under our name, or under colour of having it from an angel himself, you must conclude that you are imposed upon: and whoever preaches another gospel lays himself under a curse, and is in danger of laying you under it too."
entries.19e4c47f70a94a5a5af49d638d6367bf6640a8e0: <div eID="gen31666" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Integrity. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 56.)</title> <div sID="gen31667" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ. <hi type="super">11</hi> But I certify you, brethren, that the gospel which was preached of me is not after man. <hi type="super">12</hi> For I neither received it of man, neither was I taught <hi type="italic">it,</hi> but by the revelation of Jesus Christ. <hi type="super">13</hi> For ye have heard of my conversation in time past in the Jews' religion, how that beyond measure I persecuted the church of God, and wasted it: <hi type="super">14</hi> And profited in the Jews' religion above many my equals in mine own nation, being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of my fathers. <hi type="super">15</hi> But when it pleased God, who separated me from my mother's womb, and called <hi type="italic">me</hi> by his grace, <hi type="super">16</hi> To reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the heathen; immediately I conferred not with flesh and blood: <hi type="super">17</hi> Neither went I up to Jerusalem to them which were apostles before me; but I went into Arabia, and returned again unto Damascus. <hi type="super">18</hi> Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and abode with him fifteen days. <hi type="super">19</hi> But other of the apostles saw I none, save James the Lord's brother. <hi type="super">20</hi> Now the things which I write unto you, behold, before God, I lie not. <hi type="super">21</hi> Afterwards I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia; <hi type="super">22</hi> And was unknown by face unto the churches of Judæa which were in Christ: <hi type="super">23</hi> But they had heard only, That he which persecuted us in times past now preacheth the faith which once he destroyed. 24 And they glorified God in me. <div eID="gen31667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31668" type="x-p"/> What Paul had said more generally, in the preface of this epistle, he now proceeds more particularly to enlarge upon. There he had declared himself to be an apostle of Christ; and here he comes more directly to support his claim to that character and office. There were some in the churches of Galatia who were prevailed with to call this in question; for those who preached up the ceremonial law did all they could to lessen Paul's reputation, who preached the pure gospel of Christ to the Gentiles: and therefore he here sets himself to prove the divinity both of his mission and doctrine, that thereby he might wipe off the aspersions which his enemies had cast upon him, and recover these Christians into a better opinion of the gospel he had preached to them. This he gives sufficient evidence of, <div eID="gen31668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31669" type="x-p"/> I. From the scope and design of his ministry, which was <hi type="italic">not to persuade men, but God,</hi> &c. The meaning of this may be either that in his preaching the gospel he did not act in obedience to men, but God, who had called him to this work and office; or that his aim therein was to bring persons to the obedience, not of men, but of God. As he professed to act by a commission from God; so that which he chiefly aimed at was to promote his glory, by recovering sinners into a state of subjection to him. And as this was the great end he was pursuing, so, agreeably hereunto, <hi type="italic">he did not seek to please men.</hi> He did not, in his doctrine, accommodate himself to the humours of persons, either to gain their affection or to avoid their resentment; but his great care was to approve himself to God. The judaizing teachers, by whom these churches were corrupted, had discovered a very different temper; they mixed works with faith, and the law with the gospel, only to please the Jews, whom they were willing to court and keep in with, that they might escape persecution. But Paul was a man of another spirit; he was not so solicitous to please them, nor to mitigate their rage against him, as to alter the doctrine of Christ either to gain their favour or to avoid their fury. And he gives this very good reason for it, that, <hi type="italic">if he yet pleased men, he would not be the servant of Christ.</hi> These he knew were utterly inconsistent, and that no man could serve two such masters; and therefore, though he would not needlessly displease any, yet he dared not allow himself to gratify men at the expense of his faithfulness to Christ. Thus, from the sincerity of his aims and intentions in the discharge of his office, he proves that he was truly an apostle of Christ. And from this his temper and behaviour we may note, 1. That the great end which ministers of the gospel should aim at is to bring men to God. 2. That those who are faithful will not seek to please men, but to approve themselves to God. 3. That they must not be solicitous to please men, if they would approve themselves faithful servants to Christ. But, if this argument should not be thought sufficient, he goes on to prove his apostleship, <div eID="gen31669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31670" type="x-p"/> II. From the manner wherein he received the gospel which he preached to them, concerning which he assures them (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.11-Gal.1.12">v. 11, 12</reference>) that he had it not by information from others, but by revelation from heaven. One thing peculiar in the character of an apostle was that he had been called to, and instructed for, this office immediately by Christ himself. And in this he here shows that he was by no means defective, whatever his enemies might suggest to the contrary. Ordinary ministers, as they receive their call to preach the gospel by the mediation of others, so it is by means of the instruction and assistance of others that they are brought to the knowledge of it. But Paul acquaints them that he had his knowledge of the gospel, as well as his authority to preach it, directly from the Lord Jesus: the gospel which he preached was not <hi type="italic">after man; he neither received it of man, nor was he taught it by man,</hi> but by immediate inspiration, or revelation from Christ himself. This he was concerned to make out, to prove himself an apostle: and to this purpose, <div eID="gen31670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31671" type="x-p"/> 1. He tells them what his education was, and what, accordingly, his conversation in time past had been, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.13-Gal.1.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Particularly, he acquaints them that he had been brought up in the Jewish religion, and <hi type="italic">that he had profited in it above many his equals of his own nation</hi>—that <hi type="italic">he had been exceedingly zealous of the traditions of the elders,</hi> such doctrines and customs as had been invented by their fathers, and conveyed down from one generation to another; yea, to such a degree that, in his zeal for them, <hi type="italic">he had beyond measure persecuted the church of God, and wasted it.</hi> He had not only been a rejecter of the Christian religion, notwithstanding the many evident proofs that were given of its divine origin; but he had been a persecutor of it too, and had applied himself with the utmost violence and rage to destroy the professors of it. This Paul often takes notice of, for the magnifying of that free and rich grace which had wrought so wonderful a change in him, whereby of so great a sinner he was made a sincere penitent, and from a persecutor had become an apostle. And it was very fit to mention it here; for it would hence appear that he was not led to Christianity, as many others are, purely by education, since he had been bred up in an enmity and opposition to it; and they might reasonably suppose that it must be something very extraordinary which had made so great a change in him, which had conquered the prejudices of his education, and brought him not only to profess, but to preach, that doctrine, which he had before so vehemently opposed. <div eID="gen31671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31672" type="x-p"/> 2. In how wonderful a manner he was turned from the error of his ways, brought to the knowledge and faith of Christ, and appointed to the office of an apostle, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.15-Gal.1.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. This was not done in an ordinary way, nor by ordinary means, but in an extraordinary manner; for, (1.) God had <hi type="italic">separated him hereunto from his mother's womb:</hi> the change that was wrought in him was in pursuance of a divine purpose concerning him, whereby he was appointed to be a Christian and an apostle, before he came into the world, or had done either good or evil. (2.) he was <hi type="italic">called by his grace.</hi> All who are savingly converted are called by the grace of God; their conversion is the effect of his good pleasure concerning them, and is effected by his power and grace in them. But there was something peculiar in the case of Paul, both in the suddenness and in the greatness of the change wrought in him, and also in the manner wherein it was effected, which was not by the mediation of others, as the instruments of it, but by Christ's personal appearance to him, and immediate operation upon him, whereby it was rendered a more special and extraordinary instance of divine power and favour. (3.) He had Christ <hi type="italic">revealed in him.</hi> He was not only revealed to him, but in him. It will but little avail us to have Christ revealed to us if he is not also revealed in us; but this was not the case of Paul. It pleased God <hi type="italic">to reveal his Son in him,</hi> to bring him to the knowledge of Christ and his gospel by special and immediate revelation. And, (4.) It was with this design, that he should preach him among the heathen; not only that he should embrace him himself, but preach him to others; so that he was both a Christian and an apostle by revelation. <div eID="gen31672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31673" type="x-p"/> 3. He acquaints them how he behaved himself hereupon, from <reference osisRef="Gal.1.16">v. 16</reference>, to the end. Being thus called to his work and office, <hi type="italic">he conferred not with flesh and blood.</hi> This may be taken more generally, and so we may learn from it that, when God calls us by his grace, we must not consult flesh and blood. But the meaning of it here is that he did not consult men; he did not apply to any others for their advice and direction; <hi type="italic">neither did he go up to Jerusalem, to those that were apostles before him,</hi> as though he needed to be approved by them, or to receive any further instructions or authority from them: but, instead of that, he steered another course, and <hi type="italic">went into Arabia,</hi> either as a place of retirement proper for receiving further divine revelations, or in order to preach the gospel there among the Gentiles, being appointed to be the apostle of the Gentiles; and thence <hi type="italic">he returned again to Damascus,</hi> where he had first begun his ministry, and whence he had with difficulty escaped the rage of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.20-Acts.9.25">Acts ix</reference>. It was not till <hi type="italic">three years after</hi> his conversion that <hi type="italic">he went up to Jerusalem, to see Peter;</hi> and when he did so he made but a very short stay with him, no more than <hi type="italic">fifteen days;</hi> nor, while he was there, did he go much into conversation; for <hi type="italic">others of the apostles he saw none, but James, the Lord's brother.</hi> So that it could not well be pretended that he was indebted to any other either for his knowledge of the gospel or his authority to preach it; but it appeared that both his qualifications for, and his call to, the apostolic office were extraordinary and divine. This account being of importance, to establish his claim to this office, to remove the unjust censures of his adversaries, and to recover the Galatians from the impressions they had received to his prejudice, he confirms it by a solemn oath (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.20">v. 20</reference>), declaring, as in the presence of God, that what he had said was strictly true, and that he had not in the least falsified in what he had related, which, though it will not justify us in solemn appeals to God upon every occasion, yet shows that, in matters of weight and moment, this may sometimes not only be lawful, but duty. After this he acquaints them that <hi type="italic">he came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia:</hi> having made this short visit to Peter, he returns to his work again. He had no communication at that time with the <hi type="italic">churches of Christ in Judea,</hi> they had not so much as <hi type="italic">seen his face; but, having heard that he who persecuted them in times past now preached the faith which he once destroyed, they glorified God</hi> because of him; thanksgivings were rendered by many unto God on that behalf; the very report of this mighty change in him, as it filled them with joy, so it excited them to give glory to God on the account of it.  <chapter eID="Gal.1"/> <div eID="gen31673" type="x-p"/>

entries.67963bba71209a669555230aa142e90a303ee4c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17422"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen34855" type="x-p"/> The internal and external evidence for Paul's authorship is conclusive. The style is characteristically Pauline. The superscription, and allusions to the apostle of the Gentiles in the first person, throughout the Epistle, establish the same truth (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.1">Ga 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13-1Cor.1.24">13-24</reference>; 2:1-14). His authorship is also upheld by the unanimous testimony of the ancient Church: compare Irenæus [Against Heresies, 3,7,2] (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.19">Ga 3:19</reference>); Polycarp [Epistle to the Philippians, 3] quotes <reference osisRef="Gal.4.26">Ga 4:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">6:7</reference>; Justin Martyr, or whoever wrote the Discourse to the Greeks, alludes to <reference osisRef="Gal.4.12">Ga 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.20">5:20</reference>.<div eID="gen34855" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34854" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34856" type="x-p"/> The Epistle was written "TO THE CHURCHES OF Galatia" (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.2">Ga 1:2</reference>), a district of Asia Minor, bordering on Phrygia, Pontus, Bithynia, Cappadocia, and Paphlagonia. The inhabitants (Gallo-græci, contracted into Galati, another form of the name Celts) were Gauls in origin, the latter having overrun Asia Minor after they had pillaged Delphi, about 280 B.C. and at last permanently settled in the central parts, thence called Gallo-græcia or Galatia. Their character, as shown in this Epistle, is in entire consonance with that ascribed to the Gallic race by all writers. Cæsar [Commentaries on the Gallic War, 4,5], "The infirmity of the Gauls is that they are fickle in their resolves and fond of change, and not to be trusted." So Thierry (quoted by Alford), "Frank, impetuous, impressible, eminently intelligent, but at the same time extremely changeable, inconstant, fond of show, perpetually quarrelling, the fruit of excessive vanity." They received Paul at first with all joy and kindness; but soon wavered in their allegiance to the Gospel and to him, and hearkened as eagerly now to Judaizing teachers as they had before to him (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.14-Gal.4.16">Ga 4:14-16</reference>). The apostle himself had been the first preacher among them (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.6">Ac 16:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.8">Ga 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.13">4:13</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13">Ga 4:13</reference>; "on account of infirmity of flesh I preached unto you at the first": implying that sickness detained him among them); and had then probably founded churches, which at his subsequent visit he "strengthened" in the faith (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.23">Ac 18:23</reference>). His first visit was about A.D. 51, during his second missionary journey. Josephus [Antiquities, 16.62] testifies that many Jews resided in Ancyra in Galatia. Among these and their brethren, doubtless, as elsewhere, he began his preaching. And though subsequently the majority in the Galatian churches were Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.8">Ga 4:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">9</reference>), yet these were soon infected by Judaizing teachers, and almost suffered themselves to be persuaded to undergo circumcision (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.6">Ga 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.2">5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.12">6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.13">13</reference>). Accustomed as the Galatians had been, when heathen, to the mystic worship of Cybele (prevalent in the neighboring region of Phrygia), and the theosophistic doctrines connected with that worship, they were the more readily led to believe that the full privileges of Christianity could only be attained through an elaborate system of ceremonial symbolism (Ga 4:9-11; 5:7-12). They even gave ear to the insinuation that Paul himself observed the law among the Jews, though he persuaded the Gentiles to renounce it, and that his motive was to keep his converts in a subordinate state, excluded from the full privileges of Christianity, which were enjoyed by the circumcised alone (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.11">Ga 5:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.16">Ga 4:16</reference>, compare with <reference osisRef="Gal.2.17">Ga 2:17</reference>); and that in "becoming all things to all men," he was an interested flatterer (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.10">Ga 1:10</reference>), aiming at forming a party for himself: moreover, that he falsely represented himself as an apostle divinely commissioned by Christ, whereas he was but a messenger sent by the Twelve and the Church at Jerusalem, and that his teaching was now at variance with that of Peter and James, "pillars" of the Church, and therefore ought not to be accepted.<div eID="gen34856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34857" type="x-p"/> His PURPOSE, then, in writing this Epistle was: (1) to defend his apostolic authority (Ga 1:11-19; 2:1-14); (2) to counteract the evil influence of the Judaizers in Galatia (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.1-Gal.4.31">Ga 3:1-4:31</reference>), and to show that their doctrine destroyed the very essence of Christianity, by lowering its spirituality to an outward ceremonial system; (3) to give exhortation for the strengthening of Galatian believers in faith towards Christ, and in the fruits of the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.1-Gal.6.18">Ga 5:1-6:18</reference>). He had already, face to face, testified against the Judaizing teachers (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.9">Ga 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.16">4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.18.23">Ac 18:23</reference>); and now that he has heard of the continued and increasing prevalence of the evil, he writes with his own hand (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.11">Ga 6:11</reference>: a labor which he usually delegated to an amanuensis) this Epistle to oppose it. The sketch he gives in it of his apostolic career confirms and expands the account in Acts and shows his independence of human authority, however exalted. His protest against Peter in <reference osisRef="Gal.2.14-Gal.2.21">Ga 2:14-21</reference>, disproves the figment, not merely of papal, but even of that apostle's supremacy; and shows that Peter, save when specially inspired, was fallible like other men.<div eID="gen34857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34858" type="x-p"/> There is much in common between this Epistle and that to the Romans on the subject of justification by faith only, and not by the law. But the Epistle to the Romans handles the subject in a didactic and logical mode, without any special reference; this Epistle, in a controversial manner, and with special reference to the Judaizers in Galatia.<div eID="gen34858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34859" type="x-p"/> The STYLE combines the two extremes, sternness. (Ga 1:1-24; 3:1-5) and tenderness (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.19">Ga 4:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.20">20</reference>), the characteristics of a man of strong emotions, and both alike well suited for acting on an impressible people such as the Galatians were. The beginning is abrupt, as was suited to the urgency of the question and the greatness of the danger. A tone of sadness, too, is apparent, such as might be expected in the letter of a warm-hearted teacher who had just learned that those whom he loved were forsaking his teachings for those of perverters of the truth, as well as giving ear to calumnies against himself.<div eID="gen34859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34860" type="x-p"/> The TIME OF WRITING was after the visit to Jerusalem recorded in <reference osisRef="Acts.15.1">Ac 15:1</reference>, &c.; that is, A.D. 50, if that visit be, as seems probable, identical with that in <reference osisRef="Gal.2.1">Ga 2:1</reference>. Further, as <reference osisRef="Gal.1.9">Ga 1:9</reference> ("as we said before"), and <reference osisRef="Gal.4.16">Ga 4:16</reference> ("Have [Alford] I become your enemy?" namely, at my second visit, whereas I was welcomed by you at my first visit), refer to his second visit (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.23">Ac 18:23</reference>), this Epistle must have been written after the date of that visit (the autumn of A.D. 54). <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13">Ga 4:13</reference>, "Ye know how ... I preached ... at the first" (Greek, "at the former time"), implies that Paul, at the time of writing, had been twice in Galatia; and <reference osisRef="Gal.1.6">Ga 1:6</reference>, "I marvel that ye are so soon removed," implies that he wrote not long after having left Galatia for the second time; probably in the early part of his residence at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.23">Ac 18:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.19.1">19:1</reference>, &c., from A.D. 54, the autumn, to A.D. 57, Pentecost) [Alford]. Conybeare and Howson, from the similarity between this Epistle and that to the Romans, the same line of argument in both occupying the writer's mind, think it was not written till his stay at Corinth (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.2">Ac 20:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.3">3</reference>), during the winter of 57-58, whence he wrote his Epistle to the Romans; and certainly, in the theory of the earlier writing of it from Ephesus, it does seem unlikely that the two Epistles to the Corinthians, so dissimilar, should intervene between those so similar as the Epistles to the Galatians and Romans; or that the Epistle to the Galatians should intervene between the second to the Thessalonians and the first to the Corinthians. The decision between the two theories rests on the words, "so soon." If these be not considered inconsistent with little more than three years having elapsed since his second visit to Galatia, the argument, from the similarity to the Epistle to the Romans, seems to me conclusive. This to the Galatians seems written on the urgency of the occasion, tidings having reached him at Corinth from Ephesus of the Judaizing of many of his Galatian converts, in an admonitory and controversial tone, to maintain the great principles of Christian liberty and justification by faith only; that to the Romans is a more deliberate and systematic exposition of the same central truths of theology, subsequently drawn up in writing to a Church with which he was personally unacquainted. See on <reference osisRef="Gal.1.6">Ga 1:6</reference>, for Birks's view. Paley [Horæ Paulinæ] well remarks how perfectly adapted the conduct of the argument is to the historical circumstances under which the Epistle was written! Thus, that to the Galatians, a Church which Paul had founded, he puts mainly upon authority; that to the Romans, to whom he was not personally known, entirely upon argument.<div eID="gen34860" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gal.1.1-Gal.1.24">Ga 1:1-24</reference>. Superscription. Greetings. The Cause of His Writing Is Their Speedy Falling Away from the Gospel He Taught. Defense of His Teaching:</title> <div sID="gen34861" type="x-p"/> His Apostolic Call Independent of Man.<div eID="gen34861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34862" type="x-p"/> Judaizing teachers had persuaded the Galatians that Paul had taught them the new religion imperfectly, and at second hand; that the founder of their church himself possessed only a deputed commission, the seal of truth and authority being in the apostles at Jerusalem: moreover, that whatever he might profess among them, he had himself at other times, and in other places, given way to the doctrine of circumcision. To refute this, he appeals to the history of his conversion, and to the manner of his conferring with the apostles when he met them at Jerusalem; that so far was his doctrine from being derived from them, or they from exercising any superiority over him, that they had simply assented to what he had already preached among the Gentiles, which preaching was communicated, not by them to him, but by himself to them [Paley]. Such an apologetic Epistle could not be a later forgery, the objections which it meets only coming out incidentally, not being obtruded as they would be by a forger; and also being such as could only arise in the earliest age of the Church, when Jerusalem and Judaism still held a prominent place.<div eID="gen34862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34863" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17422"/><hi type="bold">1. apostle--</hi>in the earliest Epistles, the two to the Thessalonians, through humility, he uses no title of authority; but associates with him "Silvanus and Timotheus"; yet here, though "brethren" (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.2">Ga 1:2</reference>) are with him, he does not name them but puts his own name and apostleship prominent: evidently because his apostolic commission needs now to be vindicated against deniers of it.<div eID="gen34863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of--</hi>Greek, "from." Expressing the origin from which his mission came, "not from men," but from Christ and the Father (understood) as the source. "By" expresses the immediate operating agent in the call. Not only was the call from God as its ultimate source, but by Christ and the Father as the immediate agent in calling him (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.15">Ac 22:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.16-Acts.26.18">26:16-18</reference>). The laying on of Ananias' hands (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.17">Ac 9:17</reference>) is no objection to this; for that was but a sign of the fact, not an assisting cause. So the Holy Ghost calls him specially (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.2">Ac 13:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.3">3</reference>); he was an apostle before this special mission.<div eID="gen34864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34865" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">man--</hi>singular; to mark the contrast to "Jesus Christ." The opposition between "Christ" and "man," and His name being put in closest connection with God the Father, imply His Godhead.<div eID="gen34865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">raised him from the dead--</hi>implying that, though he had not seen Him in His humiliation as the other apostles (which was made an objection against him), he had seen and been constituted an apostle by Him in His resurrection power (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.18">Mt 28:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Ro 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.5">5</reference>). Compare as to the ascension, the consequence of the resurrection, and the cause of His giving "apostles," <reference osisRef="Eph.4.11">Ep 4:11</reference>. He rose again, too, for our justification (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.25">Ro 4:25</reference>); thus Paul prepares the way for the prominent subject of the Epistle, justification in Christ, not by the law. <div eID="gen34866" type="x-p"/>
entries.50e62deef509e2b91500cc3fde18042f2e869e70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17423"/><div sID="gen34867" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17423"/><hi type="bold">2. all the brethren--</hi>I am not alone in my doctrine; all my colleagues in the Gospel work, travelling with me (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.29">Ac 19:29</reference>, Gaius and Aristarchus at Ephesus: <reference osisRef="Acts.20.4">Ac 20:4</reference>, Sopater, Secundus, Timotheus, Tychicus, Trophimus, some, or all of these), join with me. Not that these were joint authors with Paul of the Epistle: but joined him in the sentiments and salutations. The phrase, "all the brethren," accords with a date when he had many travelling companions, he and they having to bear jointly the collection to Jerusalem [Conybeare and Howson].<div eID="gen34867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34868" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the churches--</hi>Pessinus and Ancyra were the principal cities; but doubtless there were many other churches in Galatia (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.23">Ac 18:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.1">1Co 16:1</reference>). He does not attach any honorable title to the churches here, as elsewhere, being displeased at their Judaizing. See First Corinthians; First Thessalonians, &c. The first Epistle of Peter is addressed to Jewish Christians sojourning in Galatia (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.1">1Pe 1:1</reference>), among other places mentioned. It is interesting thus to find the apostle of the circumcision, as well as the apostle of the uncircumcision, once at issue (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.7-Gal.2.15">Ga 2:7-15</reference>), co-operating to build up the same churches. <div eID="gen34868" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ed8fc54d152ba4e979d97ba726586d5b24f7fee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17424"/><div sID="gen34869" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17424"/><hi type="bold">3. from ... from--</hi>Omit the second "from." The Greek joins God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ in closet union, by there being but the one preposition. <div eID="gen34869" type="x-p"/>
entries.17e5fbe9afd3a2b98aeadfcd9cbb19bc6e4739ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17425"/><div sID="gen34870" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17425"/><hi type="bold">4. gave himself--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>); unto death, as an offering. Found only in this and the Pastoral Epistles. The Greek is different in <reference osisRef="Eph.5.25">Ep 5:25</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="Eph.5.25">Ep 5:25</reference>).<div eID="gen34870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34871" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for our sins--</hi>which enslaved us to the present evil world.<div eID="gen34871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34872" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deliver us from this--</hi>Greek, "out of the," &c. The Father and Son are each said to "deliver us," &c. (<reference osisRef="Col.1.13">Col 1:13</reference>): but the Son, not the Father, gave Himself for us in order to do so, and make us citizens of a better world (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>). The Galatians in desiring to return to legal bondage are, he implies, renouncing the deliverance which Christ wrought for us. This he more fully repeats in <reference osisRef="Gal.3.13">Ga 3:13</reference>. "Deliver" is the very word used by the Lord as to His deliverance of Paul himself (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.17">Ac 26:17</reference>): an undesigned coincidence between Paul and Luke.<div eID="gen34872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34873" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">world--</hi>Greek, "age"; system or course of the world, regarded from a religious point of view. The present age opposes the "glory" (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.5">Ga 1:5</reference>) of God, and is under the authority of the Evil One. The "ages of ages" (Greek, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.5">Ga 1:5</reference>) are opposed to "the present evil age."<div eID="gen34873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to the will of God and our Father--</hi>Greek, "of Him who is at once God [the sovereign Creator] and our Father" (<reference osisRef="John.6.38">Joh 6:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.39">39</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.18">10:18</reference>, end). Without merit of ours. His sovereignty as "God," and our filial relation to Him as "OUR Father," ought to keep us from blending our own legal notions (as the Galatians were doing) with His will and plan. This paves the way for his argument. <div eID="gen34874" type="x-p"/>
entries.152bdd72242ed8518001b93b7688e05063e96ddc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17426"/><div sID="gen34875" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17426"/><hi type="bold">5. be glory--</hi>rather, as Greek, "be the glory"; the glory which is peculiarly and exclusively His. Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Eph.3.21">Ep 3:21</reference>. <div eID="gen34875" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c1a8fbc1dcfbe3e063084d3dc32e21e0a1e06dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17427"/><div sID="gen34876" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17427"/>6. Without the usual expressions of thanksgiving for their faith, &c., he vehemently plunges into his subject, zealous for "the glory" of God (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.5">Ga 1:5</reference>), which was being disparaged by the Galatians falling away from the pure Gospel of the "grace" of God.<div eID="gen34876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34877" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I marvel--</hi>implying that he had hoped better things from them, whence his sorrowful surprise at their turning out so different from his expectations.<div eID="gen34877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so soon--</hi>after my last visit; when I hoped and thought you were untainted by the Judaizing teachers. If this Epistle was written from Corinth, the interval would be a little more than three years, which would be "soon" to have fallen away, if they were apparently sound at the time of his visit. <reference osisRef="Gal.4.18">Ga 4:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.20">20</reference> may imply that he saw no symptom of unsoundness then, such as he hears of in them now. But English Version is probably not correct there. See see on <reference osisRef="Gal.4.18">Ga 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.20">Ga 4:20</reference>; also see Introduction. If from Ephesus, the interval would be not more than one year. Birks holds the Epistle to have been written from Corinth after his FIRST visit to Galatia; for this agrees best with the "so soon" here: with <reference osisRef="Gal.4.18">Ga 4:18</reference>, "It is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing, and not only when I am present with you." If they had persevered in the faith during three years of his first absence, and only turned aside after his second visit, they could not be charged justly with adhering to the truth only when he was present: for his first absence was longer than both his visits, and they would have obeyed longer in his "absence" than in his "presence." But if their decline had begun immediately after he left them, and before his return to them, the reproof will be just. But see on <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13">Ga 4:13</reference>.<div eID="gen34878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">removed--</hi>Translate, "are being removed," that is, ye are suffering yourselves so soon (whether from the time of my last visit, or from the time of the first temptation held out to you) [Paræus] to be removed by Jewish seducers. Thus he softens the censure by implying that the Galatians were tempted by seducers from without, with whom the chief guilt lay: and the present, "ye are being removed," implies that their seduction was only in process of being effected, not that it was actually effected. Wahl, Alford, and others take the Greek as middle voice. "ye are removing" or "passing over." "Shifting your ground" [Conybeare and Howson]. But thus the point of Paul's oblique reference to their misleaders is lost; and in <reference osisRef="Heb.7.12">He 7:12</reference> the Greek is used passively, justifying its being taken so here. On the impulsiveness and fickleness of the Gauls (another form of Kel-t-s, the progenitors of the Erse, Gauls, Cymri, and Belgians), whence the Galatians sprang, see Introduction and Cæsar [Commentaries on the Gallic War, 3.19].<div eID="gen34879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from him that called you--</hi>God the Father (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.15">Ga 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.8">Ga 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.30">Ro 8:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">1Co 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.12">1Th 2:12</reference>; 5:24).<div eID="gen34880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34881" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into--</hi>rather, as Greek, "IN the grace of Christ," as the element in which, and the instrument by which, God calls us to salvation. Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.15">1Co 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.15">Ro 5:15</reference>, "the gift by (Greek, 'in') grace (Greek, 'the grace') of (the) one man." "The grace of Christ," is Christ's gratuitously purchased and bestowed justification, reconciliation, and eternal life.<div eID="gen34881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">another--</hi>rather, as Greek, "a second and different gospel," that is, into a so-called gospel, different altogether from the only true Gospel. <div eID="gen34882" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d0248d6ea8762672fb92ce0aec887686738731b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17428"/><div sID="gen34883" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17428"/><hi type="bold">7. another--</hi>A distinct Greek word from that in <reference osisRef="Gal.1.6">Ga 1:6</reference>. Though I called it a gospel (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.6">Ga 1:6</reference>), it is not really so. There is really but one Gospel, and no other gospel.<div eID="gen34883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34884" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but--</hi>Translate, "Only that there are some that trouble you," &c. (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.10">Ga 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.12">12</reference>). All I meant by the "different gospel" was nothing but a perversion by "some" of the one Gospel of Christ.<div eID="gen34884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">would pervert--</hi>Greek, "wish to pervert"; they could not really pervert the Gospel, though they could pervert Gospel professors (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">Ga 4:9</reference>, 17, 21; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.12">6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>). Though acknowledging Christ, they insisted on circumcision and Jewish ordinances and professed to rest on the authority of other apostles, namely, Peter and James. But Paul recognizes no gospel, save the pure Gospel. <div eID="gen34885" type="x-p"/>
entries.99d41827dfe47f7a6af8516c73eaa409692ccf31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17429"/><div sID="gen34886" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17429"/><hi type="bold">8. But--</hi>however weighty they may seem "who trouble you." Translate as Greek, "Even though we," namely, I and the brethren with me, weighty and many as we are (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.1">Ga 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2</reference>). The Greek implies a case supposed which never has occurred.<div eID="gen34886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34887" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angel--</hi>in which light ye at first received me (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.4.14">Ga 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.1">1Co 13:1</reference>), and whose authority is the highest possible next to that of God and Christ. A new revelation, even though seemingly accredited by miracles, is not to be received if it contradict the already existing revelation. For God cannot contradict Himself (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.1-Deut.13.3">De 13:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.18">1Ki 13:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">Mt 24:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.9">2Th 2:9</reference>). The Judaizing teachers sheltered themselves under the names of the great apostles, James, John, and Peter: "Do not bring these names up to me, for even if an angel," &c. Not that he means, the apostles really supported the Judaizers: but he wishes to show, when the truth is in question, respect of persons is inadmissible [Chrysostom].<div eID="gen34887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">preach--</hi>that is, "should preach."<div eID="gen34888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34889" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">any other gospel ... than--</hi>The Greek expresses not so much "any other gospel different from what we have preached," as, "any gospel BESIDE that which we preached." This distinctly opposes the traditions of the Church of Rome, which are at once besides and against (the Greek includes both ideas) the written Word, our only "attested rule." <div eID="gen34889" type="x-p"/>
entries.241097e297e63a080be032257f8ddb28a87aabd5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17430"/><div sID="gen34890" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17430"/><hi type="bold">9. said before--</hi>when we were visiting you (so "before" means, <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.2">2Co 13:2</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Gal.5.2">Ga 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.21">3, 21</reference>. Translate, "If any man preacheth unto you any gospel BESIDE that which," &c. Observe the indicative, not the subjunctive or conditional mood, is used, "preacheth," literally, "furnisheth you with any gospel." The fact is assumed, not merely supposed as a contingency, as in <reference osisRef="Gal.1.8">Ga 1:8</reference>, "preach," or "should preach." This implies that he had already observed (namely, during his last visit) the machinations of the Judaizing teachers: but his surprise (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.6">Ga 1:6</reference>) now at the Galatians being misled by them, implies that they had not apparently been so then. As in <reference osisRef="Gal.1.8">Ga 1:8</reference> he had said, "which we preached," so here, with an augmentation of the force, "which ye received"; acknowledging that they had truly accepted it.<div eID="gen34890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34891" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">accursed--</hi>The opposite appears in <reference osisRef="Gal.6.16">Ga 6:16</reference>. <div eID="gen34891" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ea7ba76652354a05ddcf166e081fe065610e376: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17431"/><div sID="gen34892" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17431"/><hi type="bold">10. For--</hi>accounting for the strong language he has just used.<div eID="gen34892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">do I now--</hi>resuming the "now" of <reference osisRef="Gal.1.9">Ga 1:9</reference>. "Am I now persuading men?" [Alford], that is, conciliating. Is what I have just now said a sample of men-pleasing, of which I am accused? His adversaries accused him of being an interested flatterer of men, "becoming all things to all men," to make a party for himself, and so observing the law among the Jews (for instance, circumcising Timothy), yet persuading the Gentiles to renounce it (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.11">Ga 5:11</reference>) (in order to flatter those, really keeping them in a subordinate state, not admitted to the full privileges which the circumcised alone enjoyed). Neander explains the "now" thus: Once, when a Pharisee, I was actuated only by a regard to human authority and to please men (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.15">Lu 16:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.44">Joh 5:44</reference>), but NOW I teach as responsible to God alone (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.3">1Co 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen34893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">or God?--</hi>Regard is to be had to God alone.<div eID="gen34894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for if I yet pleased men--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "for." "If I were still pleasing men," &c. (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.26">Lu 6:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.19">Joh 15:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.4">1Th 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.4">Jas 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.5">1Jo 4:5</reference>). On "yet," compare <reference osisRef="Gal.5.11">Ga 5:11</reference>.<div eID="gen34895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">servant of Christ--</hi>and so pleasing Him in all things (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.9">Tit 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.22">Col 3:22</reference>). <div eID="gen34896" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd82692d1b1ee99cb0e71bb16956d787711ff439: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17432"/><div sID="gen34897" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17432"/><hi type="bold">11. certify--</hi>I made known to you as to the Gospel which was preached by me, that it is not after man, that is, not of, by, or from man (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.1">Ga 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>). It is not according to man; not influenced by mere human considerations, as it would be, if it were of human origin.<div eID="gen34897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brethren--</hi>He not till now calls them so. <div eID="gen34898" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4f89a65cddbd12b27bc4f3d50117141bbe64ea8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17433"/><div sID="gen34899" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17433"/>12. Translate, "For not even did I myself (any more than the other apostles) receive it from man, nor was I taught it (by man)." "Received it," implies the absence of labor in acquiring it. "Taught it," implies the labor of learning.<div eID="gen34899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the revelation of Jesus Christ--</hi>Translate, "by revelation of [that is, from] Jesus Christ." By His revealing it to me. Probably this took place during the three years, in part of which he sojourned in Arabia (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.17">Ga 1:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>), in the vicinity of the scene of the giving of the law; a fit place for such a revelation of the Gospel of grace, which supersedes the ceremonial law (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.25">Ga 4:25</reference>). He, like other Pharisees who embraced Christianity, did not at first recognize its independence of the Mosaic law, but combined both together. Ananias, his first instructor, was universally esteemed for his legal piety and so was not likely to have taught him to sever Christianity from the law. This severance was partially recognized after the martyrdom of Stephen. But Paul received it by special revelation (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23">1Co 11:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.3">15:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.15">1Th 4:15</reference>). A vision of the Lord Jesus is mentioned (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.18">Ac 22:18</reference>), at his first visit to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.18">Ga 1:18</reference>); but this seems to have been subsequent to the revelation here meant (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.1.15-Gal.1.18">Ga 1:15-18</reference>), and to have been confined to giving a particular command. The vision "fourteen years before" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1">2Co 12:1</reference>) was in A.D. 43, still later, six years after his conversion. Thus Paul is an independent witness to the Gospel. Though he had received no instruction from the apostles, but from the Holy Ghost, yet when he met them his Gospel exactly agreed with theirs. <div eID="gen34900" type="x-p"/>
entries.6eeedb4c194ffce84c10c1fff4055cd2c13aa6c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17434"/><div sID="gen34901" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17434"/><hi type="bold">13. heard--</hi>even before I came among you.<div eID="gen34901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34902" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">conversation--</hi>"my former way of life."<div eID="gen34902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jews' religion--</hi>The term, "Hebrew," expresses the language; "Jew," the nationality, as distinguished from the Gentiles; "Israelite," the highest title, the religious privileges, as a member of the theocracy.<div eID="gen34903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the church--</hi>Here singular, marking its unity, though constituted of many particular churches, under the one Head, Christ.<div eID="gen34904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of God--</hi>added to mark the greatness of his sinful alienation from God (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.19">1Co 15:19</reference>).<div eID="gen34905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wasted--</hi>laid it waste: the opposite of "building it up." <div eID="gen34906" type="x-p"/>
entries.56cfeb32133d931b42092cc6cd3414c4ac19b0a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17435"/><div sID="gen34907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17435"/><hi type="bold">14. profited--</hi>Greek, "I was becoming a proficient"; "I made progress."<div eID="gen34907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">above--</hi>beyond.<div eID="gen34908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my equals--</hi>Greek, "Of mine own age, among my countrymen."<div eID="gen34909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">traditions of my fathers--</hi>namely, those of the Pharisees, Paul being "a Pharisee, and son of a Pharisee" (<reference osisRef="Acts.23.6">Ac 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.5">26:5</reference>). "MY fathers," shows that it is not to be understood generally of the traditions of the nation. <div eID="gen34910" type="x-p"/>
entries.a00306950b879c90c3b21f4707613df44ee46911: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17436"/><div sID="gen34911" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17436"/><hi type="bold">15. separated--</hi>"set me apart": in the purposes of His electing love (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.9.15">Ac 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.22.14">22:14</reference>), in order to show in me His "pleasure," which is the farthest point that any can reach in inquiring the causes of his salvation. The actual "separating" or "setting apart" to the work marked out for him, is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Acts.13.2">Ac 13:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.1">Ro 1:1</reference>. There is an allusion, perhaps, in the way of contrast, to the derivation of Pharisee from Hebrew, "pharash," "separated." I was once a so-called Pharisee or Separatist, but God had separated me to something far better.<div eID="gen34911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34912" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from ... womb--</hi>Thus merit in me was out of the question, in assigning causes for His call from <reference osisRef="Acts.9.11">Ac 9:11</reference>. Grace is the sole cause (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.9">Psa 22:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.71.6">71:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.1">Is 49:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.1.5">Jr 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.15">Lu 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen34912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">called me--</hi>on the way to Damascus (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.3-Acts.9.8">Ac 9:3-8</reference>). <div eID="gen34913" type="x-p"/>
entries.e88632e5afbac16283cd0dadb609299f5229d5c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17437"/><div sID="gen34914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17437"/><hi type="bold">16. reveal his Son in me--</hi>within me, in my inmost soul, by the Holy Spirit (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2Co 4:6</reference>, "shined in our hearts." The revealing of His Son by me to the Gentiles (so translate for "heathen") was impossible, unless He had first revealed His Son in me; at first on my conversion, but especially at the subsequent revelation from Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.12">Ga 1:12</reference>), whereby I learned the Gospel's independence of the Mosaic law.<div eID="gen34914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that I might preach--</hi>the present in the Greek, which includes the idea "that I may preach Him," implying an office still continuing. This was the main commission entrusted to him (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.7">Ga 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen34915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34916" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">immediately--</hi>connected chiefly with "I went into Arabia" (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.17">Ga 1:17</reference>). It denotes the sudden fitness of the apostle. So <reference osisRef="Acts.9.20">Ac 9:20</reference>, "Straightway he preached Christ in the synagogue."<div eID="gen34916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I conferred not--</hi>Greek, "I had not further (namely, in addition to revelation) recourse to ... for the purpose of consulting." The divine revelation was sufficient for me [Bengel].<div eID="gen34917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34918" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flesh and blood--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.16.17">Mt 16:17</reference>). <div eID="gen34918" type="x-p"/>
entries.14b63dded7ad6798429547e7edb7795294fdfffa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17438"/><div sID="gen34919" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17438"/><hi type="bold">17. went I up--</hi>Some of the oldest manuscripts read, "went away."<div eID="gen34919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to Jerusalem--</hi>the seat of the apostles.<div eID="gen34920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34921" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into Arabia--</hi>This journey (not recorded in Acts) was during the whole period of his stay at Damascus, called by Luke (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.23">Ac 9:23</reference>), "many [Greek, a considerable number of] days." It is curiously confirmatory of the legitimacy of taking "many days" to stand for "three years," that the same phrase exactly occurs in the same sense in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.38">1Ki 2:38</reference>, 39. This was a country of the Gentiles; here doubtless he preached as he did before and after (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.20">Ac 9:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.22">22</reference>) at Damascus: thus he shows the independence of his apostolic commission. He also here had that comparative retirement needed, after the first fervor of his conversion, to prepare him for the great work before him. Compare Moses (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.29">Ac 7:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.30">30</reference>). His familiarity with the scene of the giving of the law, and the meditations and revelations which he had there, appear in <reference osisRef="Gal.4.24">Ga 4:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.25">25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.18">He 12:18</reference>. See on <reference osisRef="Gal.1.12">Ga 1:12</reference>. The Lord from heaven communed with him, as He on earth in the days of His flesh communed with the other apostles.<div eID="gen34921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">returned--</hi>Greek "returned back again." <div eID="gen34922" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a67a814527aa9418e18cb9204075dc0d31bb2dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17439"/><div sID="gen34923" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17439"/><hi type="bold">18. after three years--</hi>dating from my conversion, as appears by the contrast to "immediately" (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.16">Ga 1:16</reference>). This is the same visit to Jerusalem as in <reference osisRef="Acts.9.26">Ac 9:26</reference>, and at this visit occurred the vision (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.17">Ac 22:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.22.18">18</reference>). The incident which led to his leaving Damascus (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.25">Ac 9:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.33">2Co 11:33</reference>) was not the main cause of his going to Jerusalem. So that there is no discrepancy in the statement here that he went "to see Peter"; or rather, as Greek, "to make the acquaintance of"; "to become personally acquainted with." The two oldest manuscripts read, "Cephas," the name given Peter elsewhere in the Epistle, the Hebrew name; as Peter is the Greek (<reference osisRef="John.1.42">Joh 1:42</reference>). Appropriate to the view of him here as the apostle especially of the Hebrews. It is remarkable that Peter himself, in his Epistles, uses the Greek name Peter, perhaps to mark his antagonism to the Judaizers who would cling to the Hebraic form. He was prominent among the apostles, though James, as bishop of Jerusalem, had the chief authority there (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.18">Mt 16:18</reference>).<div eID="gen34923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34924" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abode--</hi>or "tarried" [Ellicott].<div eID="gen34924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34925" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fifteen days--</hi>only fifteen days; contrasting with the long period of three years, during which, previously, he had exercised an independent commission in preaching: a fact proving on the face of it, how little he owed to Peter in regard to his apostolical authority or instruction. The Greek for "to see," at the same time implies visiting a person important to know, such as Peter was. The plots of the Jews prevented him staying longer (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.29">Ac 9:29</reference>). Also, the vision directing him to depart to the Gentiles, for that the people of Jerusalem would not receive his testimony (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.17">Ac 22:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.22.18">18</reference>). <div eID="gen34925" type="x-p"/>
entries.85767082ae499fb1f898f83a833a21cdbf3839eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17440"/><div sID="gen34926" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17440"/>19. Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.9.27">Ac 9:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.28">28</reference>, wherein Luke, as an historian, describes more generally what Paul, the subject of the history, himself details more particularly. The history speaks of "apostles"; and Paul's mention of a second apostle, besides Peter, reconciles the Epistle and the history. At Stephen's martyrdom, and the consequent persecution, the other ten apostles, agreeably to Christ's directions, seem to have soon (though not immediately, <reference osisRef="Acts.8.14">Ac 8:14</reference>) left Jerusalem to preach elsewhere.
